lines.text: The cocktail bar has evolved from a niche establishment into a cornerstone of Britain's urban nightlife and social culture. Modern cocktail bars range from speakeasy-style venues hidden behind unmarked doors to glamorous rooftop bars with panoramic city views. The bartender — or mixologist, as skilled practitioners prefer — stands behind a polished bar lined with bottles, shakers, and garnishes. A well-stocked back bar displays spirits arranged by category: gin, vodka, rum, whisky, tequila, and an array of liqueurs and bitters. The cocktail menu is curated with the care of a restaurant wine list — each drink tells a story through its combination of spirits, mixers, fresh ingredients, and presentation. Classic cocktails — the Old Fashioned, Negroni, Martini, and Daiquiri — remain staples, while seasonal and signature creations showcase the bartender's creativity. Ice is treated with reverence: large, clear cubes melt slowly and dilute drinks less than crushed or standard ice. Glassware matters too — coupes for stirred cocktails, highballs for long drinks, rocks glasses for spirit-forward serves. The garnish completes the visual and aromatic experience: a twist of citrus peel, a sprig of rosemary, or an edible flower. Cocktail culture in Britain has been democratised by home bartending trends, cocktail delivery kits, and television shows celebrating mixology as a craft.

Card payments have made tipping easier with digital prompts, though it remains more optional than in restaurants.
